5.subject: Botany
5.text: Why are vascular bundles closed in monocots?
options: Xylem and phloem occur in separate bundles.
Vascular cambium is present between xylem and phloem.
5.sol: The vascular system consists of complex tissues, the phloem and the xylem. The xylem and phloem together constitute vascular bundles. In dicotyledonous stems, cambium is present between phloem and xylem. Such vascular bundles because of the presence of cambium possess the ability to form secondary xylem and phloem tissues, and hence are called open vascular bundles. In the monocotyledons, the vascular bundles have no cambium present in them. Hence, since they do not form secondary tissues so they are referred to as closed.
5.meta: Why are vascular bundles closed in monocots?

3020.subject: Chemistry
3020.text:
Given $k_p$ for the reaction
$\frac{1}{2} C(g) \rightleftharpoons \frac{1}{2} A(g)+\frac{1}{2} B(g)$ at a fixed temperature is $0.25 \mathrm{ atm}^{-2}$. Find the $K_p$ for the reaction
$A(g)+B(g) \rightleftharpoons C(g)$ at the same temperature.
3020.sol:
For the reaction,
$\frac{1}{2} C(g) \rightleftharpoons \frac{1}{2} A(g)+\frac{1}{2} B(g)$
Given, $K_p=0.25 \mathrm{ atm}^{-2}$
We know that, $K_C=\frac{[\text{ Product }]^b}{[\text{ Reactant }]^a}$, where $a and b$ are stiochiometric coefficients.
Also, $K_p=K_C(R T)^{\Delta n_g}$
where, $\Delta n_g=b-a$
For above reaction, $K_{C_1}=\frac{[A]^{0.5}[B]^{0.5}}{[C]^{0.5}}\Delta n_g=1-0.5=0.5$
So, $K_{p_1}=K_{C_1}(R T)^{0.5}...(i)$
Similarly for reaction,
$A(g)+B(g) \rightleftharpoons C(g)$, at same temperature
$\begin{aligned}
K_{C_2} & =\frac{[C]}{[A][B]} \\
\Delta n_g & =1-2=-1 \\
K_{p_2} & =K_{C_2}(R T)^{-1}...(ii)
\end{aligned}$
Now, divide $K_{p_1} and K_{p_2}$, we get,
$\frac{K_{p_1}}{K_{p_2}}=\frac{K_{C_1}[R T]^{0.5}}{K_{C_2}[R T]^{-1}} \Rightarrow K_{p_2}=16 \mathrm{ atm}$
So, $K_p$ for the reaction
$A(g)+B(g) \rightleftharpoons C(g) \text{ is } 16 \text{ atm. }$

7605.subject: Mathematics
7605.text: Let $f$ be defined on $D = \mathbb{R} - { - 1, 1 }$ by $f\left(x\right) = \dfrac{| x |}{1 - | x |}$,& then
options: $f$ is continuous but not differentiable on $D$
$f$ is differentiable but not continuous on $D$
7605.sol:
Given:

$f ( x ) = \dfrac{| x |}{1 - | x |}$

Now,

$\text{LHL} = \lim_{x \to {0}^{-}}f\left(x\right)$

        $= \lim_{h \to 0}f\left(0 - h\right)$

        $= \lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{\left|0 - h\right|}{1 - \left|0 - h\right|} = 0$

$\text{RHL} = \lim_{x \to {0}^{+}}f\left(x\right)$

          $= \lim_{h \to 0}f\left(0 + h\right)$

           $= \lim_{h \to 0}\dfrac{\left|0 + h\right|}{1 - \left|0 + h\right|} = 0$

$\lim_{x \to {0}^{-}}f\left(x\right) = \lim_{x \to {0}^{+}}f\left(x\right) = f\left(0\right)$

Hence, $f\left(x\right)$ is continuous at $x = 0$.

Using differentiation:

$f\left(x\right) = \left\{\begin{array}{ll}\dfrac{- x}{1 + x}, x 0\end{array}\right)

${f}^{'}\left(x\right) = \left\{\begin{array}{ll}\dfrac{- 1}{1 + x} + \dfrac{x}{{\left(1 + x\right)}^{2}}; x 0\end{array}\right)

${f}^{'}\left(x\right) = \left\{\begin{array}{ll}\dfrac{- 1}{{\left(1 + x\right)}^{2}}; x 0\end{array}\right)

$\text{LHD} \ne \text{RHD}$ at $x = 0$.

Hence, $f\left(x\right)$ is differentiable in $D$ except at $x = 0$.

The electric field lines originates from a positive charge and ends at a negative charge and these field lines are also known as electric lines of forces. The direction of electric filed lines is from positive to negative.&

One of the properties of the electric lines of forces is, the tangent drawn at a point& on the electric field gives the direction of electric force.

Therefore, the electric field lines never form a closed-loop because if they do, there will be two directions of forces at the point of intersection which is not possible for electric lines of forces.

Force experienced by a charge $q$ in an electric field is, $F = qE$if the charge is $- q$or negative test change then force is$F = - qE.$& Thus, a& negative test charge experiences a force opposite to the direction of the field.

Option (i) and (iii) are true

14722.text: At what height from surface of earth the value of acceleration due to gravity will fall to half that on the surface of the earth?
14722.sol:
If \(g\) be the gravitational acceleration on the surface of earth, then gravitational acceleration at height \(h\) given as
$$\begin{aligned}& g_h=\frac{g}{\left(1+\frac{h}{R_e}\right)^2}\\
& \text{But, } g_h=\frac{g}{2}\\
& \therefore \quad \frac{g}{2}=\frac{g}{\left(1+\frac{h}{R_e}\right)^2}\\
& \Rightarrow \quad\left(1+\frac{h}{R_e}\right)^2=2 \\
& \Rightarrow \quad 1+\frac{h}{R_e}=\sqrt{2}\\
& \Rightarrow \quad h=(\sqrt{2}-1) R_e \\
& =(1.414-1) 6400 \\
& =2649.6 \mathrm{ km}\\
& \simeq 2625 \mathrm{ km}\\
\end{aligned}$$\)

\gamma_1=C_p / C_V=7 / 5

$\text{ and }$& v_2 & =$\sqrt{\frac{\gamma_2 R T}{M_2}}...($ii)
\end{array}

Dividing Eq. (i) by Eq. (ii), we get

$\frac{v_1}{v_2}=\sqrt{\frac{\gamma_1 R T}{M_1}} \times \sqrt{\frac{M_2}{\gamma_2 R T}}=\sqrt{\frac{\gamma_1}{\gamma_2} \times \frac{M_2}{M_1}}$Substituting the values, we get

$\frac{460}{v_2}=\sqrt{\frac{7}{5} \times \frac{4}{32} \times \frac{3}{5}} \Rightarrow$v_2=1420 $\mathrm{~m}$/ $\mathrm{s}$Hence, speed of sound in helium gas at the same temperature is $1420 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$.

19561.subject: Chemistry
19561.text: What is/are the product/s formed when Benzaldehyde and Ethanal react in presence of dil. $\mathrm{NaOH}$ followed by heating the intermediate product formed?
19561.sol:
The reaction between Benzaldehyde (C_{6}H_{5}CHO$) and Ethanal (CH_{3}CHO$) in the presence of dilute $NaOH$ is a crossed aldol condensation. Since Benzaldehyde has no $\alpha$-hydrogen, it acts as the electrophile, while Ethanal acts as the nucleophile.

The initial aldol addition product is $C_{6}H_{5}CH(OH)CH_{2}CHO$ (3-hydroxy-3-phenylpropanal). Upon heating, this undergoes dehydration to form 3-phenylprop-2-enal (cinnamaldehyde).

Additionally, Ethanal can undergo self-aldol condensation in the presence of dilute $NaOH$ to form $CH_{3}CH(OH)CH_{2}CHO$ (3-hydroxybutanal). Upon heating, this dehydrates to form but-2-enal (crotonaldehyde).

Therefore, the products formed are 3-phenylprop-2-enal and but-2-enal.

Answer: 3-Phenylprop-2-enal & But-2-enal

20003.subject: Chemistry
20003.text:
Given below are 4 statements. Two of these are correct statements. Identify them.
A. $\mathrm{Co}^{2+}$ is easily oxidised to $\mathrm{Co}^{3+}$ in the presence of a strong ligand like $\mathrm{CN}^{-}$
B. $[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_6]^{4-}$ is an octahedral complex ion which is paramagnetic in nature.
C. Removal of $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$ molecules from $[\mathrm{Ti}(\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O})_6] \mathrm{Cl}_3$ on strong heating converts it to a colourless compound.
D. Crystal Field splitting in Octahedral and Tetrahedral complexes is given by the equation $\Delta_0=4 / 9 \Delta_t$
20003.sol:
Statement A is correct. In the presence of strong field ligands like $\mathrm{CN}^{-}$, the crystal field splitting energy is high, which stabilizes the $\mathrm{Co}^{3+}$ oxidation state ($d^6$ configuration) over $\mathrm{Co}^{2+}$ ($d^7$ configuration) due to the large crystal field stabilization energy (CFSE).

Statement B is incorrect. $[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_6]^{4-}$ contains $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$ ($d^6$). $\mathrm{CN}^{-}$ is a strong field ligand, causing pairing of electrons in the $t_{2g}$ orbitals. Thus, it is diamagnetic, not paramagnetic.

Statement C is correct. $[\mathrm{Ti}(\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O})_6] \mathrm{Cl}_3$ is a $d^1$ complex which is violet in color. Upon strong heating, the water ligands are removed to form anhydrous $\mathrm{TiCl}_3$, which is colorless as the $d-d$ transition is no longer possible in the absence of the ligand field.

Statement D is incorrect. The relationship between octahedral splitting ($\Delta_0$) and tetrahedral splitting ($\Delta_t$) is given by $\Delta_t = \dfrac{4}{9} \Delta_0$, or $\Delta_0 = \dfrac{9}{4} \Delta_t$.

Answer: A & C

20007.subject: Chemistry
20007.text: Choose the incorrect statement from the following.
options: A tetrahedral complex of the type $[\mathrm{Ma}_2 \mathrm{b}_2]$ does not show geometrical isomerism
In a coordination entity of the type $[\mathrm{Ma} 2(\mathrm{bb})_2]^{2+}$ only the cis-isomer is optically active
Coordination entities of the type $[\mathrm{Ma}_3 \mathrm{b}_3]$ do not exhibit geometrical isomerism
Square planar complex Â of the type [Mabcd] has 3 possible geometrical isomers
20007.sol:
In a tetrahedral complex of the type $[Ma_2b_2]$, all positions are equivalent relative to each other, meaning there is no distinction between cis and trans positions. Thus, it does not show geometrical isomerism. This statement is correct.

For a coordination entity of the type $[Ma_2(bb)_2]^{2+}$, where $(bb)$ is a symmetrical bidentate ligand, the cis-isomer lacks a plane of symmetry and is optically active, while the trans-isomer possesses a plane of symmetry and is optically inactive. This statement is correct.

Coordination entities of the type $[Ma_3b_3]$ exhibit facial (fac) and meridional (mer) geometrical isomers. Therefore, the statement that they do not exhibit geometrical isomerism is incorrect.

A square planar complex of the type $[Mabcd]$ has three possible geometrical isomers, which are obtained by fixing one ligand and arranging the others in different positions relative to it. This statement is correct.

Answer: Coordination entities of the type $[\mathrm{Ma}_3 \mathrm{b}_3]$ do not exhibit geometrical isomerism

21177.subject: Mathematics
21177.text: If the conjugate of $(x+i y)(1-2 i)$ be $1+i$, then
21177.sol:
Given the conjugate of $(x+iy)(1-2i)$ is $1+i$.

Let $z = (x+iy)(1-2i)$. Then $\overline{z} = 1+i$.

Taking the conjugate on both sides, $z = \overline{1+i} = 1-i$.

Thus, $(x+iy)(1-2i) = 1-i$.

Dividing by $(1-2i)$, we get $x+iy = \dfrac{1-i}{1-2i}$.

To simplify, multiply the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator, which is $(1+2i)$:

$x+iy = \dfrac{(1-i)(1+2i)}{(1-2i)(1+2i)} = \dfrac{1 + 2i - i - 2i^2}{1^2 + 2^2} = \dfrac{1 + i + 2}{5} = \dfrac{3+i}{5} = \dfrac{3}{5} + i\dfrac{1}{5}$.

Comparing real and imaginary parts, $x = \dfrac{3}{5}$ and $y = \dfrac{1}{5}$.

Checking the options, $x+iy = \dfrac{1-i}{1-2i}$ matches option 2.

Answer: $x+i y=\dfrac{1-i}{1-2 i}$

21689.subject: Mathematics
21689.text: The maximum value of $P=500 x+400 y$ for the given constraints $x+y \leq 200, \quad x \geq 20, \quad y \geq 4 x, \quad y \geq 0$ is
21689.sol:
The constraints are given as:
1) $x + y \leq 200$
2) $x \geq 20$
3) $y \geq 4x$
4) $y \geq 0$

The feasible region is determined by the intersection of these lines. We find the vertices of the feasible region:

Intersection of $x = 20$ and $y = 4x$:
$x = 20$, $y = 4(20) = 80$. Vertex: $(20,80)$.

Intersection of $x + y = 200$ and $y = 4x$:
$x + 4x = 200 \Rightarrow 5x = 200 \Rightarrow x = 40$.
$y = 4(40) = 160$. Vertex: $(40,160)$.

Intersection of $x + y = 200$ and $x = 20$:
$20 + y = 200 \Rightarrow y = 180$. Vertex: $(20,180)$.

We evaluate the objective function $P = 500x + 400y$ at these vertices:

At $(20,80)$: $P = 500(20) + 400(80) = 10000 + 32000 = 42000$.

At $(40,160)$: $P = 500(40) + 400(160) = 20000 + 64000 = 84000$.

At $(20,180)$: $P = 500(20) + 400(180) = 10000 + 72000 = 82000$.

Comparing the values, the maximum value is $84000$.

Answer: 84,000

21748.subject: Mathematics
21748.text: Given the matrices $A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$, then the minor $M_{23}$ of the matrix $(A B^{-1})^{-1}$ is:
21748.sol:
Let $C = (A B^{-1})^{-1}$. Using the reversal law for matrix inverses, we have:

$C = (B^{-1})^{-1} A^{-1} = B A^{-1}$

First, we find the inverse of matrix $A$. The determinant of $A$ is:

$|A| = 1(2 - 0) - 0 + 1(0 - 1) = 1$

The adjugate matrix of $A$ is the transpose of its cofactor matrix. Since $A$ is symmetric, $\text{adj}(A)$ is also symmetric:

$\text{adj}(A) = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$

Thus, $A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{|A|} \text{adj}(A) = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$

Now, we compute $C = B A^{-1}$:

$C = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$

We only need the elements of the 1st and 3rd rows of $C$ to find the minor $M_{23}$ (which is obtained by deleting the 2nd row and 3rd column):

$c_{11} = (2)(2) + (1)(0) + (0)(-1) = 4$

$c_{12} = (2)(0) + (1)(1) + (0)(0) = 1$

$c_{31} = (0)(2) + (2)(0) + (1)(-1) = -1$

$c_{32} = (0)(0) + (2)(1) + (1)(0) = 2$

The minor $M_{23}$ is the determinant of the $2 \times 2$ submatrix formed by these elements:

$M_{23} = \begin{vmatrix} c_{11} \text{ and } c_{12} \\ c_{31} \text{ and } c_{32} \end{vmatrix} = \begin{vmatrix} 4 \text{ and } 1 \\ -1 \text{ and } 2 \end{vmatrix}$

$M_{23} = (4)(2) - (1)(-1) = 8 + 1 = 9$

Answer: $9$

21842.sol:
Given the ratio ^{n+1}C_{r+1} : ^{n}C_{r} : ^{n-1}C_{r-1} = 11 : 6 : 3$.

First, consider the ratio \dfrac{^{n+1}C_{r+1}}{^{n}C_{r}} = \dfrac{11}{6}$.

Using the formula ^{n}C_{r} = $\dfrac{n!}{r!(n-r)!} , we have \dfrac{(n+1)!}{(r+1)!(n-r)!} \times \dfrac{r!(n-r)!}{n!} = \dfrac{n+1}{r+1} = \dfrac{11}{6}$.

This implies 6n + 6 = 11r + 11$, or 6n - 11r = 5$. (Equation 1)

Next, consider the ratio $\dfrac{^{n}C_{r}}{^{n-1}C_{r-1}} = \dfrac{6}{3} = 2$.

Using the formula, $\dfrac{n!}{r!(n-r)!} \times \dfrac{(r-1)!(n-r)!}{(n-1)!} = \dfrac{n}{r} = 2$.

This implies $n = 2r$. (Equation 2)

Substituting $n = 2r$ into Equation 1:

$6(2r) - 11r = 5$

$12r - 11r = 5 \Rightarrow r = 5$.

Then $n = 2(5) = 10$.

The value of $nr = 10 \times 5 = 50$.

Answer: 50

22674.subject: Physics
22674.text:
A plot of kinetic energy of emitted photoelectrons from a metal versus the frequency of incident radiation gives a straight line, the intercept of which
A. Depends on the nature of the metal used
B. Depends on the intensity of radiation
C. Depends both on the intensity and the nature of metal used
D. Is a constant and is same for all metals which is independent of the intensity of Incident radiation
22674.sol:
According to Einstein's photoelectric equation, the kinetic energy $K_{max}$ of emitted photoelectrons is given by $K_{max} = h u - \Phi$, where $h$ is Planck's constant, $ u$ is the frequency of incident radiation, and $\Phi$ is the work function of the metal.

The equation $K_{max} = h u - \Phi$ represents a straight line of the form $y = mx + c$, where $y = K_{max}$, $x = u$, $m = h$ (slope), and $c = -\Phi$ (intercept).

The intercept on the $y$-axis is $-\Phi$, which is the negative of the work function of the metal. Since the work function $\Phi$ is a characteristic property of the metal, the intercept depends solely on the nature of the metal used.

The intercept is independent of the intensity of the incident radiation, as intensity only affects the number of photoelectrons emitted, not their maximum kinetic energy.

Answer: A

26194.text:
Two point charges $-Q$ and $+Q / \sqrt{3}$ are placed in the $x y$-plane at the origin $(0,0)$ and a point $(2,0)$, respectively, as shown in the figure. 26194.sol:
Let $P$$\left(h, k\right)$ be be a general point with potential to be zero.

${V}_{1} + {V}_{2} = 0$ (as potential given $= 0$)

$\dfrac{K\left(- Q\right)}{\sqrt{{h}^{2} + {k}^{2}}} + \dfrac{K\left(\dfrac{Q}{\sqrt{3}}\right)}{\sqrt{{\left(h - 2\right)}^{2} + {k}^{2}}} = 0$

$\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}\sqrt{{\left(h - 2\right)}^{2} + {k}^{2}}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{{h}^{2} + {k}^{2}}}$

$3\left[{\left(h - 2\right)}^{2} + {k}^{2}\right] = {h}^{2} + {k}^{2}$

$3\left({h}^{2} - 4h + 4 + {k}^{2}\right) = {h}^{2} + {k}^{2}$

$2{h}^{2} + 2{k}^{2} - 12h + 12 = 0$

${h}^{2} + {k}^{2} - 6h + 6 = 0$

$\left({h}^{2} - 6h + 6\right) + {k}^{2} = 0$

$\left({h}^{2} - 6h + 9\right) + {k}^{2} = 3$

${\left(h - 3\right)}^{2} + {k}^{2} = 3$

Standard equation of circle is given by

${\left(x - {x}_{1}\right)}^{2} + {\left(y - {y}_{1}\right)}^{2} = {R}^{2}$

$∴ {x}_{1} = 3, {y}_{1} = 0$ and $R = \sqrt{3}$

Hence, $R = \sqrt{3}m$

and value of $b = 3m$

Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The first ionization enthalpy of $3d$ series elements is more than that of group $2$ metals

Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
28537.sol:
Metal $Sc$ $Ti$ $V$ $Cr$ $Mn$ $Fe$ $Co$ $Ni$ $Cu$ $Zn$
IE $( kJ / mol )$ $631$ $656$ $650$ $653$ $717$ $762$ $758$ $736$ $745$ $906$
Metal $Be$ $Mg$ $Ca$ $Sr$ $Ba$ $Ra$
IE $( kJ / mol )$ $899$ $737$ $590$ $549$ $503$ $509$

In the first transition series, the first and second ionization enthalpy values increase slowly on moving across the period. As the nuclear charge rises, the interaction between the nucleus and valence electrons increases, and as a result, the ionization enthalpy increases. So, Sc has the lowest value of ionization enthalpy while Zn has the highest value of ionization enthalpy.

So, both assertion and reasons are true and reason is the correct expalantion of assertion.

28657.subject: Chemistry
28657.text:
Given below are two statements:
Statement I: Each electron in $e_g$ orbitals destabilizes the orbitals by $+0.6\Delta_o$ and each electron in the $t_{2g}$ orbitals stabilizes the orbitals by $-0.4\Delta_o$ in an octahedral field on the basis of crystal field theory.
Statement II: All the d-orbitals of the transition metals have the same energy in their free atomic state but when a complex is formed the ligands destroy the degeneracy of these orbitals on the basis of crystal field theory.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
28657.sol:
In an octahedral crystal field, the five degenerate d-orbitals split into two sets: a lower energy $t_{2g}$ set and a higher energy $e_g$ set.

The energy of the $t_{2g}$ orbitals is lowered by $0.4\Delta_o$ (stabilization of $-0.4\Delta_o$) and the energy of the $e_g$ orbitals is raised by $0.6\Delta_o$ (destabilization of $+0.6\Delta_o$) relative to the barycenter. Hence, Statement I is correct.

In the free atomic or ionic state, all five d-orbitals of a transition metal are degenerate (have the same energy). When ligands approach the central metal ion to form a complex, the spherically symmetrical field is disrupted, which destroys the degeneracy of the d-orbitals and causes them to split. Hence, Statement II is correct.

Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.

Answer: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct

29281.subject: Chemistry
29281.text: Given at $298$ K: $E^{\ominus}_{Fe^{2+}/Fe} = X$ Volt; $E^{\ominus}_{Fe^{3+}/Fe} = Y$ Volt. The $E^{\ominus}_{Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}}$ in Volt at $298$ K is given by:
29281.sol:
The half-reactions and their standard Gibbs free energy changes are given by:

$Fe^{2+} + 2e^{-} \rightarrow Fe$

$\Delta G^{\ominus}_{1} = -2FX$

$Fe^{3+} + 3e^{-} \rightarrow Fe$

$\Delta G^{\ominus}_{2} = -3FY$

The required half-reaction is:

$Fe^{3+} + e^{-} \rightarrow Fe^{2+}$

$\Delta G^{\ominus}_{3} = -1FE^{\ominus}_{Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}}$

This reaction is obtained by subtracting the first reaction from the second reaction:

$\Delta G^{\ominus}_{3} = \Delta G^{\ominus}_{2} - \Delta G^{\ominus}_{1}$

$-FE^{\ominus}_{Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}} = -3FY - (-2FX)$

$-FE^{\ominus}_{Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}} = -3FY + 2FX$

$E^{\ominus}_{Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}} = 3Y - 2X$

Answer: $3Y-2X$

Circle of radius 4 passes through O and points A($-\sqrt{3a}$, 0), B(0, $-\sqrt{2b}$).
Let center be C(h, k) on circle: $h^2 + k^2 = 16$.
Since A, B lie on circle: $3a^2 + 2\sqrt{3a}h + h^2 + k^2 = 16$ gives $h = -\frac{\sqrt{3a}}{2}$
And $h^2 + 2b + 2\sqrt{2b}k + k^2 = 16$ gives $k = -\frac{\sqrt{2b}}{2}$
Centroid G = $\left(\frac{-\sqrt{3a}}{3}, \frac{-\sqrt{2b}}{3}\right)$. Setting $x = \frac{-\sqrt{3a}}{3}$ and $y = \frac{-\sqrt{2b}}{3}$:
a = 3x^2 and $b = \frac{9y^2}{2}$
From $h^2 + k^2 = 16$: $\frac{3a}{4} + \frac{2b}{4} = 16$ → $3a + 2b = 64$
Substituting: $9x^2 + 9y^2 = 64$ → $x^2 + y^2 = \frac{64}{9}$
Radius = $\frac{8}{3}$

So we can write

$e{V}_{2} = \dfrac{{\left(\dfrac{h}{1 . 5\lambda}\right)}^{2}}{2m} . . . Eq ( 2 )$

From both equations, we get

$\dfrac{{V}_{1}}{{V}_{2}} = {\left(1 . 5\right)}^{2} = \dfrac{9}{4}$

48957.subject: Mathematics
48957.text: The slope of the tangent to the curve \( x=t^{2}+3 t-8, y=2 t^{2}-2 t-5 \) at the point \( (2,-1) \) is
48957.sol:
Given that, $x=t^{2}+3 t-8 \rightarrow(1)y=2 t^{2}-2 t-5 \rightarrow(2)$
At point $(2,-1)$, Eq. (2) becomes
$-1=2 t^{2}-2 t-5\Rightarrow 2 t^{2}-2 t-4=0\Rightarrow t^{2}-t-2=0\Rightarrow(t-2)(t+1)=0\Rightarrow t=2,-1 \rightarrow(3)$
Similarly, at point $(2,-1)$ Eq. (1) becomes
$2=t^{2}+3 t-8\Rightarrow t^{2}+3 t-10=0\Rightarrow(t+5)(t-2)=0\Rightarrow t=2,-5 \rightarrow(4)$
From Eqs. (3) and (4), we have common value of $t=2$
Now, $\frac{d y}{d t}=4 t-2$ and $\frac{d x}{d t}=2 t+3$
So, slope of the tangent to the curve is
$\frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{4 t-2}{2 t+3}\Rightarrow\left(\frac{d y}{d x}\right)_{t=2}=\frac{4(2)-2}{(2)+3}=\frac{6}{7}$

49456.subject: Mathematics
49456.text: The sum of the series, $\frac{1}{2.3} \cdot 2+\frac{2}{3.4} \cdot 2^{2}+\frac{3}{4.5} \cdot 2^{3}+\ldots$ upto $n$ terms is
49456.sol:
Given series is $\frac{1}{2 \cdot 3} \cdot 2^{1}+\frac{2}{3.4} \cdot 2^{2}+\frac{3}{4.5} \cdot 2^{3}+\ldots$ upto $n$ terms The $n$th term of the series is
$T_{n}=\frac{n}{(n+1)(n+2)} \cdot 2^{n}=\left\{\frac{2 \cdot 2^{n}}{(n+2)}-\frac{2^{n}}{(n+1)}\right\}$
On putting $n=1,2,3 \ldots$, we get
$T_{1}=2 \cdot \frac{2^{1}}{3}-\frac{2^{1}}{2}, T_{2}=\frac{2 \cdot 2^{2}}{4}-\frac{2^{2}}{3}, T_{3}=\frac{2 \cdot 2^{3}}{5}-\frac{2^{3}}{4}$
On adding, we get
$\begin{aligned}
&\quad S_{n}=T_{1}+T_{2}+T_{3}+\ldots+T_{n} \\
&\Rightarrow \quad S_{n}=\frac{2 \cdot 2^{n}}{(n+2)}-\frac{2}{2}=\frac{2^{n+1}}{(n+2)}-1
\end{aligned}$

55772.subject: Chemistry
55772.text: Identify the different types of bonds present in quaternary ammonium salts.
55772.sol:
Quaternary ammonium salts have the general formula $R_4N^+ X^-$.

The bonds present within the alkyl or aryl groups (R$) and three of the nitrogen-carbon bonds are covalent.

The fourth nitrogen-carbon bond is formed by the donation of the lone pair of electrons from the nitrogen atom to an electron-deficient carbon atom, which is a co-ordinate (dative) bond.

The electrostatic force of attraction between the complex quaternary ammonium cation (R_4N^+$) and the counter anion (X^-$) constitutes an ionic bond.

Thus, quaternary ammonium salts contain covalent, co-ordinate, and ionic bonds.

Answer: covalent, co-ordinate and ionic$

55988.text: In first order reaction 20 millimole of reactant is reduced to 10 millimole in $1 \cdot 151$ minute. Find rate constant.
55988.sol:
For a first order reaction, the rate constant is given by

$k = \dfrac{2 \cdot 303}{t} \log \left( \dfrac{a}{a-x} \right)

Substituting the given values $ a = 20$ millimole, $a-x = 10$ millimole, and $t = 1 $\cdot151$ minute:

$k = \dfrac{2 \cdot 303}{1 \cdot 151} \log \left( \dfrac{20}{10} \right)

$ k = $\dfrac{2 \cdot 303}{1 \cdot 151} \log2$

$k = \dfrac{2 \cdot 303 \times 0 \cdot 3010}{1 \cdot 151}

$ k = 0 $\cdot6023 \text{ minute}^{-1}

Answer: 0 $\cdot$6023 \text{ minute}^{-1}$

The differential equation $x \frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} + y \log x = x e^{x} x^{-1/2} \log x$ is rearranged into standard linear form by dividing through by $x$, yielding

$\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} + \frac{\log x}{x} y = e^{x} x^{-3/2} \log x$

From this, $P(x) = \frac{\log x}{x}$. The integrating factor is $e^{\int P(x) \, \mathrm{d}x} = e^{\int \frac{\log x}{x} \, \mathrm{d}x}$.

Using the substitution $u = \log x$, $\mathrm{d}u = \frac{1}{x} \, \mathrm{d}x$, the integral evaluates to $\frac{(\log x)^{2}}{2}$, so the integrating factor simplifies to $e^{(\log x)^{2}/2}$.

Analyzing the options, $x^{\log x} = e^{(\log x)^{2}}$ and $(\sqrt{x})^{\log x} = e^{\frac{1}{2}(\log x)^{2}}$; only C gives the correct form. The integrating factor corresponds to choice C.

Given equation is $x^2 + 2x + 4 = 0$.

Sum of the roots, $\alpha + \beta = -2$

64372.text: If for some $m \in \mathbb{R}$ the lines $L_1 : \dfrac{x+1}{m} = \dfrac{y-m}{-1} = \dfrac{z-1}{1}$ and $L_2 : \dfrac{x+2}{-4} = \dfrac{y+1}{9} = \dfrac{z+1}{1}$ are coplanar, then line $L_1$ passes through the point
64372.sol:
For the lines $L_1$ and $L_2$ to be coplanar, the shortest distance between them must be zero. The condition for coplanarity of two lines is given by:

$\begin{vmatrix} x_2 - x_1 \text{ and } y_2 - y_1 \text{ and } z_2 - z_1 \\ a_1 \text{ and } b_1 \text{ and } c_1 \\ a_2 \text{ and } b_2 \text{ and } c_2 \end{vmatrix} = 0$

From the given equations, the lines pass through the points $(-1, m, 1)$ and $(-2, -1, -1)$ respectively. Their direction ratios are $(m, -1, 1)$ and $(-4, 9, 1)$.

Substituting these values into the determinant:

$\begin{vmatrix} -2 - (-1) \text{ and } -1 - m \text{ and } -1 - 1 \\ m \text{ and } -1 \text{ and } 1 \\ -4 \text{ and } 9 \text{ and } 1 \end{vmatrix} = 0$

$\begin{vmatrix} -1 \text{ and } -1-m \text{ and } -2 \\ m \text{ and } -1 \text{ and } 1 \\ -4 \text{ and } 9 \text{ and } 1 \end{vmatrix} = 0$

Expanding the determinant along the first row:

$-1(-1 - 9) - (-1 - m)(m - (-4)) - 2(9m - 4) = 0$

$10 + (1 + m)(m + 4) - 18m + 8 = 0$

$10 + m^2 + 5m + 4 - 18m + 8 = 0$

$m^2 - 13m + 22 = 0$

$(m - 2)(m - 11) = 0$

This gives $m = 2$ or $m = 11$.

For $m = 2$, the equation of line $L_1$ becomes:

$\dfrac{x+1}{2} = \dfrac{y-2}{-1} = \dfrac{z-1}{1}$

Checking the given options by substituting the coordinates into the equation of $L_1$ for $m = 2$:

For the point $(7, -2, 5)$:

$\dfrac{7+1}{2} = \dfrac{8}{2} = 4$

$\dfrac{-2-2}{-1} = \dfrac{-4}{-1} = 4$

$\dfrac{5-1}{1} = \dfrac{4}{1} = 4$

Since all three parts are equal, the line $L_1$ passes through the point $(7, -2, 5)$.

64842.text: If $\sin \left(\frac{\pi}{4} \cot \theta\right)=\cos \left(\frac{\pi}{4} \tan \theta\right)$, then the general solution of $\theta$ is
64842.sol:
The equation $\sin \left(\frac{\pi}{4} \cot \theta\right) = \cos \left(\frac{\pi}{4} \tan \theta\right)$ is equivalent to $\sin \left(\frac{\pi}{4} \cot \theta\right) = \sin \left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{\pi}{4} \tan \theta\right)$ using the identity $\cos x = \sin \left(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\right)$.

The general solution for $\sin A = \sin B$ is $A = n\pi + (-1)^n B$, where $n \in \mathbb{Z}$. Applying this yields $\frac{\pi}{4} \cot \theta = n\pi + (-1)^n \left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{\pi}{4} \tan \theta\right)$.

Dividing through by $\frac{\pi}{4}$ gives $\cot \theta = 4n + (-1)^n (2 - \tan \theta)$.

Assuming the arguments of sine and cosine are acute angles, $\sin A = \cos B$ implies $A = \frac{\pi}{2} - B$. Thus, $\frac{\pi}{4} \cot \theta = \frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{\pi}{4} \tan \theta$.

Multiplying both sides by $\frac{4}{\pi}$ yields $\cot \theta = 2 - \tan \theta$, which simplifies to $\cot \theta + \tan \theta = 2$.

Since $\cot \theta + \tan \theta = \frac{1}{\sin \theta \cos \theta} = \frac{2}{\sin(2\theta)}$, we obtain $\frac{2}{\sin(2\theta)} = 2$, hence $\sin(2\theta) = 1$.

The general solution is $2\theta = 2n\pi + \frac{\pi}{2}$, so $\theta = n\pi + \frac{\pi}{4}$.

This yields $\cot \theta = 1$ and $\tan \theta = 1$, confirming the acute angle assumption and satisfying the original equation.

Final answer: $\boxed{\text{A}}$

66580.subject: Physics
66580.text: The de-Broglie wavelength $(\lambda)$ of a particle
66580.sol:
The de Broglie wavelength $\lambda$ is given by $\lambda = h/p$, where $h$ is Planck's constant and $p$ is the momentum.

For a particle starting from rest, the impulse $J$ equals the final momentum $p$. Since $\lambda$ is inversely proportional to $p$, and $p$ is directly proportional to $J$, the de Broglie wavelength is inversely proportional to the impulse imparted.

The final answer is $\boxed{A}$

66585.text: A parallel beam of light is incident normally on a plane surface absorbing 50\% of the light and reflecting the rest. If the incident beam carries 90 W of power, the force exerted by it on the surface is $\left(\mathrm{C}=\right.velocity$ of light in air $\left.=3 \times 10^8 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}\right)$
66585.sol:
Given an incident power $P = 90\text{ W}$ and light velocity $c = 3 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}$, with 50% absorption and 50% reflection.

The absorbed power is $P_{\text{abs}} = 0.50 \times 90 = 45\text{ W}$, and the reflected power is $P_{\text{ref}} = 0.50 \times 90 = 45\text{ W}$.

The force due to absorbed light is $F_{\text{abs}} = \frac{45}{3 \times 10^8} = 1.5 \times 10^{-7}\text{ N}$.

For reflection, the force is $F_{\text{ref}} = \frac{2 \times 45}{3 \times 10^8} = 3 \times 10^{-7}\text{ N}$.

The total force exerted is $F_{\text{total}} = F_{\text{abs}} + F_{\text{ref}} = 4.5 \times 10^{-7}\text{ N}$.

The final answer is $\boxed{\text{A}}$.

67053.text: A conducting sphere of radius ' $R$ ' is given a charge ' $Q$ ' uniformly. The electric field and the electric potential at the centre of the sphere are respectively [\epsilon_0=$ permittivity of free space]$
67053.sol:
Electric Field at the Center
For a conducting sphere in electrostatic equilibrium, all charge resides on its outer surface. Consider a Gaussian surface with radius $r < R$ enclosing zero charge. By Gauss’s law, $\oint \mathrm{E} \cdot d\mathrm{A} = Q_{\text{enc}} / \epsilon_0 = 0$, so $E = 0$ throughout the interior, including the center.

Electric Potential at the Center
The potential is constant throughout a conductor. On the surface, $V_{\text{surface}} = Q / (4 \pi \epsilon_0 R)$, so the potential at the center is identical: $V_{\text{center}} = Q / (4 \pi \epsilon_0 R)$.

The electric field is zero and the potential is $Q / (4 \pi \epsilon_0 R)$, corresponding to option $\boxed{A}$.

68095.text:
A metal wire of length 'L' and density 'd' floats horizontally on the free surface of water. The maximum radius of the wire does not sink in water is
[T$ = surface tension of water , $g$ = gravitational acceleration]$
68095.sol:
Weight of the metal wire acting downwards is $W = \pi r^2 L d g$

Maximum upward force due to surface tension is $F = 2 T L$

For the wire to float without sinking, the maximum upward force must balance the weight of the wire.

$2 T L = \pi r^2 L d g$

$r^2 = \dfrac{2 T}{\pi d g}$

$r = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 T}{\pi d g}}$

Answer: $\sqrt{\dfrac{2T}{\pi dg}}$

68438.subject: Physics
68438.text: A boat crosses a river from one bank A to another bank B which is opposite. The distance between them is D. The speed of water is $V_W$ and that of boat relative to water is $V_B$. If $V_B = 2V_W$, the time taken by the boat to cross the river directly along AB is $\left(\sin 30^{}^{\circ} = \dfrac{1}{2}\right)$, $\left(\cos 30^{}^{\circ} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)$
68438.sol:
Let the boat be steered at an angle $\theta$ upstream with respect to the line AB to cross the river directly.

For the boat to move exactly along AB, the component of its velocity parallel to the river flow must cancel the river's velocity $V_W$.

$V_B \sin \theta = V_W$

Given $V_B = 2V_W$, substituting this yields:

$2V_W \sin \theta = V_W \Rightarrow \sin \theta = \dfrac{1}{2} \Rightarrow \theta = 30^\circ$

The net velocity of the boat along the line AB is the component of $V_B$ perpendicular to the river flow:

$V = V_B \cos \theta = V_B \cos 30^\circ = V_B \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)$

The time taken to cross the river of width $D$ is:

$t = \dfrac{D}{V} = \dfrac{D}{V_B \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}} = \dfrac{2D}{V_B \sqrt{3}}$

Answer: $\dfrac{2D}{V_B\sqrt{3}}$

69149.text:
A thin uniform rod AB of mass '$m$' and length '$l$' is hinged at one end A to the ground level. Initially the rod stands vertically and is allowed to fall freely to the ground in the vertical plane. The angular velocity of the rod when its B end strikes the ground is
(g$ = acceleration due to gravity)$
69149.sol:
By the principle of conservation of mechanical energy, the loss in potential energy of the rod is equal to the gain in its rotational kinetic energy.

The initial height of the center of mass of the rod is $h_i = \dfrac{l}{2}$ and the final height is $h_f = 0$.

Loss in potential energy $= mg \left(\dfrac{l}{2}\right)

Gain in rotational kinetic energy $= $\dfrac{1}{2} I\omega^2$

The moment of inertia of the rod about the hinged end A is $I = \dfrac{ml^2}{3}.

Equating the two energies:

$mg$\left(\dfrac{l}{2}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{ml^2}{3}\right)\omega^2$

$mgl = \dfrac{ml^2}{3} \omega^2$

\omega^2 = $\dfrac{3g}{l}

$\omega = \sqrt{$\dfrac{3g}{l}$}$

Answer: \sqrt{\dfrac{3g}{l}}$

69198.text:
A solid sphere and thin walled hollow sphere have same mass and same material. Which of them have greater moment of inertia about their diameter?
[ $\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{h}}=$ moment of inertia of hollow sphere about an axis coinciding with its diameter, $\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{s}}=$ moment of inertia of solid sphere about an axis coinciding with its diameter]
69198.sol:
The moment of inertia depends on both the mass and its distribution relative to the rotation axis. For a solid sphere of mass $M$ and radius $R$, the moment of inertia about a diameter is $I_s = \frac{2}{5}MR^2$.

For a thin-walled hollow sphere of equal mass and radius, the moment of inertia is $I_h = \frac{2}{3}MR^2$.

Since the mass in the hollow sphere is concentrated entirely at its outer surface, it is distributed farther from the axis of rotation. The coefficients confirm this relationship: $\frac{2}{3} > \frac{2}{5}$, so $I_h > I_s$.

The hollow sphere has greater moment of inertia.

70519.text: The frequency of a tuning fork is 256 Hz. It will <u>not</u> resonate with the tuning fork of frequency
70519.sol:
Resonance occurs when frequencies are exact integer multiples. Given $f_0 = 256\text{ Hz}$, the harmonic frequencies are $n \times 256\text{ Hz}$ for integer $n$.

The frequency $754\text{ Hz}$ is approximately $2.945f_0$, which is not an integer multiple of $256\text{ Hz}$ and will not resonate.$512\text{ Hz} = 2f_0$ and $768\text{ Hz} = 3f_0$ are harmonics and will resonate.

The tuning fork that does not resonate is $\boxed{\text{C}}$.

71453.subject: Biology
71453.text:
Given below are two statements:
Statement (I): The rate of glycolysis is controlled by ATP consumption, $NAD^++H^+$ regeneration and enzymes like hexokinase, pyruvate kinase etc.
Statement (II): It is also controlled by hormones like glucagon, epinephrine and insulin.
In light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below.
options: Both Statement (I) and Statement (II) are correct.
Both Statement (I) and Statement (II) are incorrect.
Statement (I) is correct but Statement (II) is incorrect.
Statement (I) is incorrect but Statement (II) is correct.
71453.sol:
Statement (I) is correct because the rate of glycolysis is fundamentally controlled by the cellular energy charge, including ATP consumption and the continuous need for $NAD^+$ regeneration from $NADH + H^+$. The process is strictly regulated by key allosteric enzymes such as hexokinase, phosphofructokinase, and pyruvate kinase.

Statement (II) is correct because glycolysis is also subject to hormonal regulation to maintain systemic blood glucose homeostasis. Hormones like insulin upregulate glycolysis by promoting the activation of regulatory enzymes, whereas glucagon and epinephrine generally inhibit glycolysis in the liver via phosphorylation cascades.

Therefore, both Statement (I) and Statement (II) are correct.

Answer: Both Statement (I) and Statement (II) are correct.

71479.subject: Biology
71479.sol:
Heteroanthy is the condition in which a plant produces flowers with stamens of different lengths. This phenomenon is characteristically associated with heterostyly, a condition where flowers have styles of different lengths.

In heterostylous plants (such as Primula), the variation in style length is always accompanied by a corresponding variation in stamen length (heteroanthy). For example, pin-eyed flowers have long styles and short stamens, while thrum-eyed flowers have short styles and long stamens. This structural adaptation facilitates cross-pollination by insects and prevents self-pollination.

Therefore, heteroanthy is always associated with heterostyly.

Answer: heterostyly

71566.subject: Biology
71566.text: Which one of the following does NOT favour absorption of water in plants?
options: Low concentration of solutes in soil water.
71566.sol:
Water absorption by plant roots is influenced by several environmental factors.

Low concentration of solutes in soil water means the soil solution is hypotonic compared to the root cell sap, creating a water potential gradient that favours water absorption.

Increased transpiration rates create a strong transpiration pull, which is the primary driving force for passive water absorption in plants.

Capillary water is the only form of soil water readily available to plants, so its presence favours absorption.

Poorly aerated soil lacks sufficient oxygen required for root respiration. This reduces the metabolic activity of root cells, inhibiting root growth and decreasing the rate of water absorption. Therefore, poorly aerated soil does not favour the absorption of water.

Answer: Poorly aerated soil.

71705.subject: Chemistry
71705.text: What is the bond angle Cl-B-Cl and molecular geometry of $\text{BCl}_3$ molecule?
71705.sol:
The central atom in $\text{BCl}_3$ is Boron (B).

The number of valence electrons in Boron is $3$. It forms $3$ single bonds with $3$ Chlorine atoms.

Number of bond pairs = $3$
Number of lone pairs = $0$

Steric number = Bond pairs + Lone pairs = $3 + 0 = 3$

A steric number of $3$ corresponds to $sp^2$ hybridization.

Since there are no lone pairs on the central atom, the molecular geometry is trigonal planar.

The bond angle for a regular trigonal planar geometry is $120^{}^{\circ}$.

Answer: $120^{}^{\circ}$ and trigonal planar

$\text{C}^5\text{H}_3\text{-C}^4\text{H=C}^3\text{H-C}^2\text{H}_2\text{-C}^1\text{OOH}$

The longest chain has $5$ carbon atoms, so the root word is pent.

There is a double bond starting at carbon $3$, so the primary suffix is $3$-en.

Combining these parts, the IUPAC name is pent-$3$-enoic acid.

Answer: Pent-3-enoic acid

72404.subject: Physics
72404.text: Assume that the temperature of the surface of the sun is $5000$ K and the surface temperature of another virtual star is $2500$ K. The power radiated by a virtual star is $30$ times the power radiated by the sun. The radius of a virtual star in terms of the radius of the sun is {Treat both the sun and the virtual star as a black body}
72404.sol:
According to the Stefan-Boltzmann law, the power radiated by a black body is given by $P = \sigma A T^4 = \sigma (4 \pi r^2) T^4$.

For the sun:
$P_{s} = \sigma (4 \pi r_{s}^2) T_{s}^4$

For the virtual star:
$P_{v} = \sigma (4 \pi r_{v}^2) T_{v}^4$

Given $P_{v} = 30 P_{s}$, we have:
$\sigma (4 \pi r_{v}^2) T_{v}^4 = 30 \sigma (4 \pi r_{s}^2) T_{s}^4$

$\dfrac{r_{v}^2}{r_{s}^2} = 30 \left( \dfrac{T_{s}}{T_{v}} \right)^4$

Substituting $T_{s} = 5000$ K and $T_{v} = 2500$ K:
$\dfrac{r_{v}^2}{r_{s}^2} = 30 \left( \dfrac{5000}{2500} \right)^4$

$\dfrac{r_{v}^2}{r_{s}^2} = 30 (2)^4 = 30 \times 16 = 480$

$r_{v} = \sqrt{480} r_{s} = 4\sqrt{30} r_{s}$

Answer: $4\sqrt{30}\,r_{sun}$

73825.subject: General Ability
73825.text: Which one of the following statements is NOT correct?
options: Half mole of nitrogen gas is measured 11.2 litre at STP
17 gram of ammonia gas contains $6.022 \times 10^{23}$ molecules at STP
22.4 litre of $CO_2$ gas at STP contains 44 gram of molecules
4 gram of hydrogen gas contains $6.022 \times 10^{23}$ molecules
73825.sol:
At STP, $1$ mole of any ideal gas occupies $22.4$ litres.

Half mole of nitrogen gas occupies $\dfrac{1}{2} \times 22.4 = 11.2$ litres. This statement is correct.

Molar mass of ammonia ($NH_3$) is $17$ g/mol. $17$ g of ammonia corresponds to $1$ mole, which contains $6.022 \times 10^{23}$ molecules. This statement is correct.

$22.4$ litres of $CO_2$ gas at STP corresponds to $1$ mole. The molar mass of $CO_2$ is $44$ g/mol, so it weighs $44$ grams. This statement is correct.

Molar mass of hydrogen gas ($H_2$) is $2$ g/mol. $4$ grams of hydrogen gas corresponds to $\dfrac{4}{2} = 2$ moles. The number of molecules in $2$ moles is $2 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 1.2044 \times 10^{24}$ molecules. This statement is incorrect.

Answer: 4 gram of hydrogen gas contains $6.022 \times 10^{23}$ molecules

77318.subject: Mathematics
77318.text:
For the following two (02) items:
Consider the function $f(x) = \dfrac{10^x - 10^{-x}}{10^x + 10^{-x}}$.

What is the inverse of the function?
77318.sol:
Let $y = f(x) = \dfrac{10^x - 10^{-x}}{10^x + 10^{-x}}$

Multiplying the numerator and the denominator by $10^x$, we get:

$y = \dfrac{10^{2x} - 1}{10^{2x} + 1}$

Applying componendo and dividendo:

$\dfrac{1 + y}{1 - y} = \dfrac{10^{2x} + 1 + 10^{2x} - 1}{10^{2x} + 1 - (10^{2x} - 1)}$

$\dfrac{1 + y}{1 - y} = \dfrac{2 \cdot 10^{2x}}{2}$

$10^{2x} = \dfrac{1 + y}{1 - y}$

Taking logarithm to the base $10$ on both sides:

$2x = \log_{10}\left(\dfrac{1 + y}{1 - y}\right)$

$x = \dfrac{1}{2}\log_{10}\left(\dfrac{1 + y}{1 - y}\right)$

Replacing $y$ with $x$ to find the inverse function:

$f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{1}{2}\log_{10}\left(\dfrac{1 + x}{1 - x}\right)$

Answer: $\dfrac{1}{2}\log_{10}\left(\dfrac{1 + x}{1 - x}\right)$

The new observations are given by $y_i = \dfrac{x_i + 5}{20} = \dfrac{1}{20}x_i + \dfrac{1}{4}$.

If a new variable is defined as $y_i = ax_i + b$, its standard deviation is given by $\sigma_y = |a|\sigma_x$.

Substituting $a = \dfrac{1}{20}$ and $\sigma_x = 10$:

$\sigma_y = \left| \dfrac{1}{20} \right| \times 10 = 0.5$

The new standard deviation is $0.5$.

Answer: $0.5$

78956.subject: Mathematics
78956.text:
Consider the following for the three (03) items that follow:
Let $p = \tan 2\alpha - \tan\alpha$ and $q = \cot\alpha - \cot 2\alpha$.

What is $(p + q)$ equal to?
78956.sol:
Given $p = \tan 2\alpha - \tan\alpha$ and $q = \cot\alpha - \cot 2\alpha$.

Simplifying $p$:
$p = \dfrac{\sin 2\alpha}{\cos 2\alpha} - \dfrac{\sin\alpha}{\cos\alpha} = \dfrac{\sin 2\alpha \cos\alpha - \cos 2\alpha \sin\alpha}{\cos 2\alpha \cos\alpha} = \dfrac{\sin(2\alpha - \alpha)}{\cos 2\alpha \cos\alpha} = \dfrac{\sin\alpha}{\cos 2\alpha \cos\alpha}$

Simplifying $q$:
$q = \dfrac{\cos\alpha}{\sin\alpha} - \dfrac{\cos 2\alpha}{\sin 2\alpha} = \dfrac{\cos\alpha \sin 2\alpha - \sin\alpha \cos 2\alpha}{\sin\alpha \sin 2\alpha} = \dfrac{\sin(2\alpha - \alpha)}{\sin\alpha \sin 2\alpha} = \dfrac{\sin\alpha}{\sin\alpha \sin 2\alpha} = \dfrac{1}{\sin 2\alpha}$

Now, adding $p$ and $q$:
$p + q = \dfrac{\sin\alpha}{\cos 2\alpha \cos\alpha} + \dfrac{1}{\sin 2\alpha}$

Using $\sin 2\alpha = 2\sin\alpha \cos\alpha$:
$p + q = \dfrac{\sin\alpha}{\cos 2\alpha \cos\alpha} + \dfrac{1}{2\sin\alpha \cos\alpha}$

$p + q = \dfrac{2\sin^2\alpha + \cos 2\alpha}{2\sin\alpha \cos\alpha \cos 2\alpha}$

Using the identity $\cos 2\alpha = 1 - 2\sin^2\alpha$ in the numerator and $2\sin\alpha \cos\alpha = \sin 2\alpha$ in the denominator:
$p + q = \dfrac{2\sin^2\alpha + (1 - 2\sin^2\alpha)}{\sin 2\alpha \cos 2\alpha}$

$p + q = \dfrac{1}{\sin 2\alpha \cos 2\alpha}$

Multiplying and dividing by $2$:
$p + q = \dfrac{2}{2\sin 2\alpha \cos 2\alpha} = \dfrac{2}{\sin 4\alpha}$

$p + q = 2\csc 4\alpha$

Answer: $2\csc 4\alpha$

In NO, total electrons $=7+8=15 \therefore$ Configuration of $\mathrm{NO}

& \therefore $\text{ Configuration$ of } $\mathrm{C}_2^{2-}$ \\
& =K K, \sigma$\left(2 s^2\right)$, \stackrel{*}{\sigma}$\left(2 s^2\right)$, \sigma$\left(2 p_z^2\right)$, \approx \pi$\left(2 p_x^2\right)$, \pi$\left(2 p_y^2\right)$ \\
& \therefore \quad $\text{ Bond order }= \frac{8-2}{2}$ \\
& =$\frac{6}{2}=$3 \\

81048.subject: Chemistry
81048.text:
For the reaction, $A+B \rightarrow$ products, it is observed that
(1) On doubling the initial concentration of $A$ only, the rate of reaction is also doubled and
(2) On doubling the initial concentrations of both $A$ and $B$, there is a change by a factor of 8 in the rate of the reaction.
The rate of this reaction is, given by
81048.sol:
For the reaction, $\mathrm{A}+\mathrm{B} \longrightarrow$ Products
On doubling the initial concentration of A only, the rate of reaction is also doubled, therefore

$\text{ Rate } \propto[\mathrm{A}]^$1

Let initially rate law is

$\text{ Rate }=$k[A][B]^y

If concentration of and both are doubled, the rate gets changed by a factor of 8 .

$\begin{array}{r}8 \times \text{ Rate }$=$\mathrm{k}$[2 $\mathrm{~A}$][2 $\mathrm{~B}$]^${\mathrm{y}}$ \quad \ldots($\text{ iii) }$\\
{$\left[\because \text{ Rate } \propto[\mathrm{A}]^1$\right]$}
\end{array}$

Dividing Eq. (iii) by Eq. (ii),

$\begin{aligned}$& 8=2 $\times$2^y \\
& 4=2^y \\
& \therefore \quad $\mathrm{y}=$2 \\
&
\end{aligned}

Hence, rate law is, rate $=\mathrm{k}[\mathrm{A}][\mathrm{B}]^2$

84821.text: Which of the following statements about lac-operon is correct ?
options: Galactose can act as an inducer of lac operon
Lactose activates repressor to bind to the operator
Genes $i$, $z$, $y$ and $a$ share single common promoter
84821.sol:
The $i$ gene in the lac operon codes for the repressor protein. It is a regulatory gene that is constitutively expressed, meaning it is transcribed continuously to maintain a basal level of repressor in the cell.

Galactose does not act as an inducer of the lac operon; lactose or allolactose serves as the inducer.

Lactose binds to the repressor protein and inactivates it, preventing it from binding to the operator region.

Genes $z$, $y$, and $a$ are structural genes that share a single common promoter, whereas the $i$ gene has its own separate promoter.

Answer: Gene $i$ is constitutively expressed

86145.subject: Chemistry
86145.text: tert-Butylbenzene reacts with 1-chloro-2-methylpropane in the presence of anhydrous $\text{AlCl}_3$. The major product in this reaction is:
86145.sol:
The reaction is a Friedel-Crafts alkylation.

First, 1-chloro-2-methylpropane reacts with anhydrous $AlCl_3$ to form a primary carbocation, the isobutyl cation:

$(CH_3)_2CH-CH_2-Cl + AlCl_3 \rightarrow (CH_3)_2CH-CH_2^+ + AlCl_4^-$

This less stable primary carbocation undergoes a 1,2-hydride shift to form a more stable tertiary carbocation, the tert-butyl cation:

$(CH_3)_2CH-CH_2^+ \rightarrow (CH_3)_3C^+$

The tert-butyl group on the starting material, tert-butylbenzene, is an ortho/para directing group.

Due to severe steric hindrance caused by the bulky tert-butyl group already present on the benzene ring, the incoming bulky tert-butyl electrophile predominantly attacks at the less hindered para position.

Therefore, the major product is 1,4-di-tert-butylbenzene, which corresponds to the structure in option (2).

Answer :

$⇒ A^{5} = A^{4} = A^{3} = A$

$B^{2} = B ⋅ B = \left(BA\right) ⋅ B = B\left(AB\right) = BA = B$
$⇒ B^{5} = B^{4} = B^{3} = B$
So, ${ \left(A + B\right)}^{2} = A^{2} + B^{2} + AB + BA = 2\left(A + B\right)$
${\left(A + B\right)}^{3} = { \left(A + B\right)}^{2} \left(A + B\right) =2{ \left(A + B\right)}^{2} = 4 \left(A + B\right)$
Similarly,
${ \left(A + B\right)}^{4} = 8 \left(A + B\right)$
${ \left(A + B\right)}^{5} = 16 \left(A + B\right)$

92498.subject: Physics
92498.text: In the spectrum of the hydrogen atom, the ratio of the wavelengths of the longest wavelength in $Lyman$ series to the longest wavelength in the $Balmer$ series is
92498.sol:
When an electron jumps& down from any higher energy level to the first energy level, then the emitted lines form the Lyman series

$\dfrac{1}{\lambdaL} = R \left(\dfrac{1}{12} - \dfrac{1}{n2}\right), where $Ris the $Rydberg constant.

Similarly, when an electron~jumps down& from any higher energy level to the second energy level, then the emitted lines form the Balmer series

\dfrac{1}{\lambdaB} =$R $\left(\dfrac{1}{22} - \dfrac{1}{n2}\right)$

For maximum wavelength, the energy gap should be the smallest

$n = 2$,~$\dfrac{1}{\lambdaL} = R\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{22}\right) = R\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{4}\right) = \dfrac{3R}{4}$

$n = 3$,~$\dfrac{1}{\lambdaB} = R\left(\dfrac{1}{22} - \dfrac{1}{32}\right) = \dfrac{5R}{36}$

$\dfrac{{λ}_{L}}{\lambdaB} = \dfrac{5}{27}$

97692.text: How many molecules of ATP will be generated in Krebs cycle, if a molecule of sucrose is completely oxidised and used as substrate?
97692.sol:
Sucrose is a disaccharide having one glucose and one fructose.

1 pyruvic acid in Kreb's cycle produces 12 ATP. One glucose molecule produces 2 pyruvate molecules in glycolysis. Fructose also enters glycolysis by forming fructose1,6 diphosphate. Therefore there will be two pyruvates from glucose and two from fructose, and each cycle producing 12 ATP. Therefore $12 \times 4 = 48$ ATP.

102242.subject: Physics
102242.text: A sample of solid carbon dioxide (dry ice) is placed in a chamber. If the intermolecular forces between the molecules were to completely vanish, the substance would occupy a volume of $11.2 \text{ m}^3$ at STP. What is the actual mass of the dry ice sample?
102242.sol:
If the intermolecular forces vanish, the substance behaves as an ideal gas.

The volume occupied by the gas at STP is given as $V = 11.2 \text{ m}^3$.
Since $1 \text{ m}^3 = 1000 \text{ L}$, the volume in liters is:
$V = 11.2 \times 10^3 \text{ L} = 11200 \text{ L}$

The volume occupied by one mole of an ideal gas at STP is $22.4 \text{ L}$.
Number of moles of $\text{CO}_2$ is:
$n = \dfrac{11200}{22.4} = 500 \text{ mol}$

The molar mass of $\text{CO}_2$ is $44 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$.
Total mass of the sample is:
$m = n \times M = 500 \times 44 = 22000 \text{ g}$

Converting to kilograms:
$m = 22 \text{ kg}$

Answer: $22 \text{ kg}$

103672.subject: Physics
103672.text: A long straight solid wire of radius $R$ carries a steady current uniformly distributed across its cross-section. The magnitude of the magnetic field at a radial distance $x$ from the axis (where $x < R$) is found to be exactly equal to the magnitude of the magnetic field at a radial distance $y$ from the axis (where $y > R$). The radius $R$ of the wire can be expressed as:
103672.sol:
Let the uniform current in the solid wire be $I$.

The magnetic field at a point inside the wire at a radial distance $x$ ($x < R$) is given by:
$B_{in} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I x}{2\pi R^2}$

The magnetic field at a point outside the wire at a radial distance $y$ ($y > R$) is given by:
$B_{out} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi y}$

Given that the magnitudes of the magnetic fields at these two points are equal:
$B_{in} = B_{out}$
$\dfrac{\mu_0 I x}{2\pi R^2} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi y}$

Cancelling the common terms $\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi}$ on both sides:
$\dfrac{x}{R^2} = \dfrac{1}{y}$

Rearranging to solve for $R$:
$R^2 = xy$
$R = \sqrt{xy}$

Answer: $\sqrt{xy}$

103708.subject: Physics
103708.text:
A straight horizontal conducting wire of uniform mass per unit length $\lambda$ carries a current $I$. Another infinitely long straight wire is kept fixed at a distance $d$ directly below it. The upper wire is free to move vertically. For the upper wire to just levitate and remain stationary, what must be the magnitude and direction of the current in the lower wire?
[$g$ is the acceleration due to gravity and $\mu_0$ is the permeability of free space.]
options: $\dfrac{\pi d \lambda g}{\mu_0 I}$ in the same direction as $I$
$\dfrac{2\pi d \lambda g}{\mu_0 I}$ in the same direction as $I$
$\dfrac{\pi d \lambda g}{\mu_0 I}$ in the opposite direction to $I$
$\dfrac{2\pi d \lambda g}{\mu_0 I}$ in the opposite direction to $I$
103708.sol:
For the upper wire to levitate, the net vertical force on it must be zero. This means the downward gravitational force must be balanced by an upward magnetic force.

Since the lower wire is fixed below the upper wire, the magnetic force exerted by the lower wire on the upper wire must be repulsive (pushing it upwards).

Two parallel current-carrying wires repel each other when their currents are in opposite directions. Therefore, the current in the lower wire must be in the opposite direction to $I$.

The downward gravitational force per unit length on the upper wire is:
$W = \lambda g$

The upward magnetic force per unit length on the upper wire due to the lower wire carrying current $I'$ is:
$F = \dfrac{\mu_0 I I'}{2\pi d}$

Equating the two forces for equilibrium:
$\dfrac{\mu_0 I I'}{2\pi d} = \lambda g$

Solving for the current $I'$ in the lower wire:
$I' = \dfrac{2\pi d \lambda g}{\mu_0 I}$

Thus, the required current is $\dfrac{2\pi d \lambda g}{\mu_0 I}$ in the opposite direction to $I$.

Answer: $\dfrac{2\pi d \lambda g}{\mu_0 I}$ in the opposite direction to $I$

104956.subject: Physics
104956.text:
Choose correct statement/statements :
(a) Nuclear force is independent of charge of nucleons.
(b) Nuclear force has saturation property.
(c) Nuclear force is always Attractive is nature.
(d) Nuclear force exists in range of femtometre.
104956.sol:
- (a) Nuclear force is independent of charge of nucleons. This statement is true. Nuclear forces act equally between proton-proton, neutron-neutron, and proton-neutron pairs.
- (b) Nuclear force has saturation property. This statement is true. A nucleon interacts only with its nearest neighbors, not with all other nucleons in the nucleus. This leads to saturation.
- (c) Nuclear force is always Attractive is nature. This statement is false. While predominantly attractive, nuclear forces become strongly repulsive at very short distances (less than about 0.7 fm), preventing the nucleus from collapsing.
- (d) Nuclear force exists in range of femtometre. This statement is true. Nuclear forces are short range forces, effective only over distances of a few femtometers (\(1 \mathrm{fm}=10^{-15} \mathrm{~m}\)).
Therefore, the correct statements are (a), (b), and (d). This corresponds to option (2).

106232.text:
According to Bohr's atomic theory:
(A) Kinetic energy of electron is $∝ \dfrac{{Z}^{2}}{{n}^{2}} .$
(B) The product of velocity (v) of electron and principal quantum number $\left(n\right), ' vn ' ∝ {Z}^{2} .$
(C) Frequency of revolution of electron in an orbit is $∝ \dfrac{{Z}^{3}}{{n}^{3}} .$
(D) Coulombic force of attraction on the electron is $∝ \dfrac{{Z}^{3}}{{n}^{4}} .$

Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
106232.sol:
According to the Bohr's atomic theory, the kinetic energy of an electron is directly proportional to the square of the atomic number and inversely proportional to the square of the principal quantum number. 

(A) $KE = 13 . 6\dfrac{{z}^{2}}{{n}^{2}}\dfrac{eV}{atom} ⇒ KE \alpha\dfrac{{z}^{2}}{{n}^{2}}$

(B) speed of ${e}^{-}\alpha\dfrac{z}{n}$

$∴ v \times n \alpha z$

(C) Frequency of revolution of ${e}^{-} = \dfrac{v}{2\pi r}$

$∴$ Frequency $\alpha\dfrac{{z}^{2}}{{n}^{3}}$

(D) Coulombic force of attraction on the electron is directly proportional to the square of the atomic number and inversely proportional to the fourth power of the principal quantum number. 

 $F = \dfrac{{kq}_{1}{q}_{2}}{{r}^{2}} = \dfrac{{kze}^{2}}{{r}^{2}}\left\{r \alpha\dfrac{{n}^{2}}{z}\right)

$⇒ F \alpha\dfrac{z}{{\left(\dfrac{{n}^{2}}{z}\right)}^{2}}$

$⇒ F \alpha\dfrac{{z}^{3}}{{n}^{4}}$

106508.subject: Chemistry
106508.text: The correct order of the decreasing ionic radii among the following isoelectronic species is
106508.sol:
Key Idea:- lonic radii $\propto$ charge on anion $\propto \frac{1}{\text{ charge on cation }}$ During the formation of a cation, the electrons are lost from the outer shell and the remaining electrons experience a great force of attraction by the nucleus, ie, attracted more towards the nucleus. In other words, nucleus hold the remaining electrons more tightly and this results in decreased radii.
However, in case of anion formation, the addition of electron(s) takes place in the same outer shell, thus the hold of nucleus on the electrons of outer shell decreases and this results in increased ionic radii.
Thus, the correct order of ionic radii is

\mathrm{S}^{2-}>$\mathrm{Cl}^{-}$>\mathrm{K}^{+}>$\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}$

107764.subject: Chemistry
107764.text: Consider the structure of the tetrathionate ion ($\text{S}_4\text{O}_6^{2-}$). What is the difference in the oxidation state between the terminal and central sulfur atoms, and what is the total number of lone pairs present on all the sulfur atoms in the ion, respectively?
107764.sol:
The tetrathionate ion ($\text{S}_4\text{O}_6^{2-}$) has the structure $^-\text{O}_3\text{S}-\text{S}-\text{S}-\text{SO}_3^-$.

The terminal sulfur atoms are bonded to three oxygen atoms and one sulfur atom. Assigning electrons based on electronegativity, the terminal sulfur atoms have an oxidation state of $+5$. The central sulfur atoms are bonded only to other sulfur atoms, so they have an oxidation state of $0$.
Difference in oxidation state $= 5 - 0 = 5$.

For lone pairs on sulfur atoms:
Terminal sulfur atoms use all $6$ of their valence electrons in bonding (two double bonds to oxygen, one single bond to oxygen, and one single bond to sulfur), leaving $0$ lone pairs.
Each central sulfur atom uses $2$ of its $6$ valence electrons to form single bonds with adjacent sulfur atoms, leaving $4$ non-bonding electrons, which corresponds to $2$ lone pairs per central sulfur atom.
Total lone pairs on all sulfur atoms $= 0 + 2 + 2 + 0 = 4$.

Therefore, the difference in oxidation state is $5$, and the total number of lone pairs on sulfur atoms is $4$.

Answer: $5$ and $4$

108731.text: In an isobaric process, when temperature changes from $T_1$ to $T_2, \Delta S$ is equal to
108731.sol:
The entropy change for a process, when $T$ and $P$ are the variables is given by
$\Delta S=C_P \ln \frac{T_2}{T_1}-R \ln \frac{P_2}{P_1}$
For an isobaric process $P_1=P_2$. Hence the above equation reduces to
$C_P \ln \frac{T_2}{T_1}=\Delta S$
or $\Delta S=2.303 C_P \log \frac{T_2}{T_1}$.

108965.subject: Chemistry
108965.text:
A mixture of $2.0\text{ moles}$ of $\text{SO}_{2}$ and $2.0\text{ moles}$ of $\text{O}_{2}$ is placed in a closed vessel of volume $2.0\text{ L}$ and allowed to reach equilibrium according to the reaction:

$2\text{SO}_{2}(\text{g}) + \text{O}_{2}(\text{g}) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{SO}_{3}(\text{g})$

At equilibrium, $1.0\text{ mole}$ of $\text{SO}_{3}$ is formed. The value of the equilibrium constant $K_{c}$ for this reaction is:
108965.sol:
Set up an ICE (Initial, Change, Equilibrium) table for the moles of each species:
Initial moles: $\text{SO}_{2} = 2.0$, $\text{O}_{2} = 2.0$, $\text{SO}_{3} = 0$

Since $1.0\text{ mole}$ of $\text{SO}_{3}$ is formed at equilibrium, the change for $\text{SO}_{3}$ is $+1.0\text{ mol}$.
From the stoichiometry of the reaction ($2:1:2$), the change in $\text{SO}_{2}$ is $-1.0\text{ mol}$ and the change in $\text{O}_{2}$ is $-0.5\text{ mol}$.

Equilibrium moles:
$\text{SO}_{2} = 2.0 - 1.0 = 1.0\text{ mol}$
$\text{O}_{2} = 2.0 - 0.5 = 1.5\text{ mol}$
$\text{SO}_{3} = 1.0\text{ mol}$

Convert moles to equilibrium concentrations by dividing by the volume of the vessel ($2.0\text{ L}$):
$[\text{SO}_{2}] = \dfrac{1.0}{2.0} = 0.5\text{ M}$
$[\text{O}_{2}] = \dfrac{1.5}{2.0} = 0.75\text{ M}$
$[\text{SO}_{3}] = \dfrac{1.0}{2.0} = 0.5\text{ M}$

Write the equilibrium constant expression:
$K_{c} = \dfrac{[\text{SO}_{3}]^{2}}{[\text{SO}_{2}]^{2}[\text{O}_{2}]}$

Substitute the equilibrium concentrations:
$K_{c} = \dfrac{(0.5)^{2}}{(0.5)^{2} \times 0.75} = \dfrac{1}{0.75} = \dfrac{4}{3} \approx 1.33$

Common mistakes:
- Using moles directly instead of concentrations gives $0.67$.
- Subtracting $1.0\text{ mol}$ from $\text{O}_{2}$ instead of $0.5\text{ mol}$ gives $2.0$.
- Inverting the $K_{c}$ expression gives $0.75$.

Answer: $1.33$

111880.text:
Match the elements detected in an organic compound (List-I) with the reagents used and the corresponding observation in their qualitative analysis (List-II).

List-I (Element)List-II (Reagent and Observation)
(A) Nitrogen(I) Sodium nitroprusside, violet colour
(B) Sulphur(II) Ammonium molybdate, yellow precipitate
(C) Halogen(III) $\mathrm{FeSO_4}$ followed by conc. $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$, Prussian blue colour
(D) Phosphorus(IV) $\mathrm{AgNO_3}$ and $\mathrm{HNO_3}$, precipitate


Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
111880.sol:
In the qualitative analysis of organic compounds:

(A) Nitrogen is detected by boiling the sodium fusion extract with $\mathrm{FeSO_4}$ and then acidifying with concentrated $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$, which yields a Prussian blue colour due to the formation of ferriferrocyanide.

(B) Sulphur is detected by adding sodium nitroprusside to the sodium fusion extract, resulting in a violet colour.

(C) Halogens are detected by acidifying the sodium fusion extract with $\mathrm{HNO_3}$ and adding $\mathrm{AgNO_3}$, which forms a precipitate (white, pale yellow, or yellow depending on the halogen).

(D) Phosphorus is detected by heating the compound with an oxidising agent (like sodium peroxide), boiling with $\mathrm{HNO_3}$, and adding ammonium molybdate to form a yellow precipitate of ammonium phosphomolybdate.

Therefore, the correct match is (A)-(III), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(II).

Answer: (A)-(III), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(II)

118810.text:
Match List-I with List-II regarding the preparation of phenol.

List-I (Substrate)List-II (Reagents/Conditions)
A. ChlorobenzeneI. Oleum, then $\mathrm{NaOH}$, $\mathrm{H}^+$
B. BenzeneII. $\mathrm{O}_2$, then $\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{O}^+$
C. AnilineIII. $\mathrm{NaOH}$ ($623\text{ K}, 300\text{ atm}$), then $\mathrm{H}^+$
D. CumeneIV. $\mathrm{NaNO}_2 + \mathrm{HCl}$ ($273-278\text{ K}$), then warm $\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}$

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
118810.sol:
Chlorobenzene is converted to phenol by Dow's process, which requires extreme conditions: $\mathrm{NaOH}$ at $623\text{ K}$ and $300\text{ atm}$, followed by acidification (A-III).

Benzene is first sulphonated with oleum to form benzene sulphonic acid, which is then fused with $\mathrm{NaOH}$ and acidified to yield phenol (B-I).

Aniline is diazotised using $\mathrm{NaNO}_2$ and $\mathrm{HCl}$ at $273-278\text{ K}$ to form benzene diazonium chloride, which on warming with water gives phenol (C-IV).

Cumene is oxidised by $\mathrm{O}_2$ to cumene hydroperoxide, which upon acid hydrolysis ($\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{O}^+$) yields phenol and acetone (D-II).

Therefore, the correct match is A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II.

Answer: A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II

119593.text: Which of the following undergoes nucleophilic substitution exclusively by $\mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{N}} 1$ mechanism?
119593.sol:
Aliphatic $S_{\mathrm{N}} 1$ reaction is carried out in two steps.
In form of slow step
Step (i) carbonium (carbocation) ion is formed and its formation is based upon the stability Stability order of carbocation
$\mathrm{C}_6 \mathrm{H}_5 \stackrel{+}{\mathrm{C}} \mathrm{H}_2\gt\mathrm{CH}_3-\stackrel{+}{\mathrm{C}} \mathrm{H}-\mathrm{CH}_3\gt\mathrm{CH}_3-\stackrel{+}{\mathrm{C}} \mathrm{H}_2$
and in step (ii) nucleophile is attracted towards the carbonium ion in form of fast step to give final product.
Hence, in benzyl chloride, ethyl chloride and isopropyl chloride order of $\mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{N}} 1$ reaction is benzyl chloride $\gt$ isopropyl chloride $\gt$ ethyl chloride
In chlorobenzene, mechanism of $S_{\mathrm{N}} 1$ reaction is differ to aliphatic alkyl halide. The aryl halides are much less reactive as compared to alkyl halides, towards nucleophilic reagents in either $S_{\mathrm{N}} 1$ or $S_{\mathrm{N}} 2$ reaction.
The carbon-halogen bond in the aryl halide is quite strong and only forcing conditions can break up this bond.
Hence,
Step (i) $\mathrm{C}_6 \mathrm{H}_5 \mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{Cl} \xrightarrow{\text{ Slow }} \mathrm{C}_6 \mathrm{H}_5 \stackrel{+}{\mathrm{C}} \mathrm{H}_2+\mathrm{Cl}^{-}$
Rate $\propto\left[\mathrm{C}_6 \mathrm{H}_5 \mathrm{CH}_2 \mathrm{Cl}\right]$
Step (ii) $\mathrm{C}_6 \mathrm{H}_5-\stackrel{+}{\mathrm{C}} \mathrm{H}_2+\mathrm{Nu}^{-} \xrightarrow{\text{ Fast }} \mathrm{C}_6 \mathrm{H}_5 \mathrm{CH}_2 \mathrm{Nu}$

123897.subject: Botany
123897.text: An animal cell with a diploid chromosome number of $2n = 16$ is undergoing mitosis. What will be the number of chromosomes and chromatids respectively in this cell during Metaphase and Anaphase?
options: Metaphase: 16 chromosomes, 32 chromatids; Anaphase: 32 chromosomes, 32 chromatids
Metaphase: 16 chromosomes, 16 chromatids; Anaphase: 32 chromosomes, 32 chromatids
Metaphase: 16 chromosomes, 32 chromatids; Anaphase: 16 chromosomes, 32 chromatids
Metaphase: 32 chromosomes, 32 chromatids; Anaphase: 16 chromosomes, 16 chromatids
123897.sol:
In a cell with $2n = 16$, the DNA replicates during the S phase, but the chromosome number remains the same. Each chromosome now consists of two sister chromatids.

During Metaphase, the chromosomes align at the equator. The centromeres have not yet split. Therefore, there are 16 chromosomes, and since each has two chromatids, there are $16 \times 2 = 32$ chromatids.

During Anaphase, the centromere of each chromosome splits. The 32 sister chromatids separate and are now referred to as daughter chromosomes. Because they are now independent entities within the same cell (before cytokinesis), the cell temporarily contains 32 chromosomes. These correspond to the 32 separated daughter chromatids.

Thus, the correct count is Metaphase: 16 chromosomes, 32 chromatids; Anaphase: 32 chromosomes, 32 chromatids.

Answer: Metaphase: 16 chromosomes, 32 chromatids; Anaphase: 32 chromosomes, 32 chromatids

125152.text: When a specific biomolecule is utilised as the primary respiratory substrate, the volume of carbon dioxide evolved is slightly less than the volume of oxygen consumed, yielding a Respiratory Quotient (RQ) of approximately 0.9. Identify the most likely substrate.
125152.sol:
The Respiratory Quotient (RQ) is defined as the ratio of the volume of $CO_2$ evolved to the volume of $O_2$ consumed during respiration.

According to NCERT, the RQ depends upon the type of respiratory substrate used during respiration. When carbohydrates are used as substrate and are completely oxidised, the RQ will be 1. When fats (like tripalmitin) are used in respiration, the RQ is less than 1 (approximately 0.7). When proteins are respiratory substrates, the ratio would be about 0.9.

Therefore, an RQ of 0.9 corresponds to proteins.

Answer: Proteins

125803.subject: Botany
125803.text: How does a typical microsporangium appear in a transverse section?
125803.sol: The bilobed nature of an anther is very distinct in the transverse section of the anther. The anther is a four-sided (tetragonal) structure consisting of four microsporangia located at the corners, two in each lobe. The microsporangia develop further and become pollen sacs. They extend longitudinally all through the length of an anther and are packed with pollen grains. Structure of microsporangium: In a transverse section, a typical microsporangium appears near circular in outline. It is generally surrounded by four wall layers the epidermis, endothecium, middle layers and the tapetum. The outer three wall layers perform the function of protection and help in dehiscence of anther to release the pollen. The innermost wall layer is the tapetum. It nourishes the developing pollen grains. Cells of the tapetum possess dense cytoplasm and generally have more than one nucleus.

126204.text:
Match List-I with List-II regarding the reproductive features of plants.

List-IList-II
(A) Papaya(1) Prevents autogamy but not geitonogamy
(B) Castor(2) Prevents both autogamy and geitonogamy
(C) Commelina(3) Produces both chasmogamous and cleistogamous flowers

126204.sol:
Papaya is a dioecious plant, meaning male and female flowers are present on different plants. This condition prevents both autogamy and geitonogamy. Thus, (A) matches with (2).

Castor is a monoecious plant, where male and female flowers are borne on the same plant. This prevents autogamy (pollination within the same flower) but not geitonogamy (pollination between different flowers of the same plant). Thus, (B) matches with (1).

Commelina produces two types of flowers: chasmogamous flowers (similar to flowers of other species with exposed anthers and stigma) and cleistogamous flowers (which do not open at all). Thus, (C) matches with (3).

Therefore, the correct matching is (A)-(2), (B)-(1), (C)-(3).

Answer: (A)-(2), (B)-(1), (C)-(3)

126269.subject: Botany
126269.text: During a field study, a researcher observes a pollinating agent transferring pollen between two distinct, open flowers. Later, genetic analysis of the resulting seeds reveals that they are genetically identical to the parent plant. Which of the following types of pollination has occurred in this scenario?
126269.sol:
The observation that pollen transfer occurred between two distinct flowers via a pollinating agent indicates functional cross-pollination. This rules out normal autogamy (which occurs within the same flower) and cleistogamy (which occurs in closed flowers that do not open at all).

The genetic analysis shows that the seeds are genetically identical to the parent plant. This means the pollen must have come from the same plant, ruling out xenogamy, which involves the transfer of pollen from a different plant and brings genetic variation.

The only type of pollination that involves two distinct flowers (requiring an agent) but results in genetically identical offspring (because both flowers are on the same plant) is geitonogamy.

Answer: Geitonogamy

128881.subject: Zoology
128881.text: What is the purpose of atrial systole in the heart?
options: To increase the flow of blood into the ventricles
To stimulate the ventricular muscles to contract
128881.sol: The ventricles now relax (ventricular diastole) and the ventricular pressure falls causing the closure of semilunar valves which prevents the backflow of blood into the ventricles. As the ventricular pressure declines further, the tricuspid and bicuspid valves are pushed open by the pressure in the atria exerted by the blood which was being emptied into them by the veins. The blood now once again moves freely to the ventricles. The ventricles and atria are now again in a relaxed (joint diastole) state, as earlier. Soon the SAN generates a new action potential and the events described above are repeated in that sequence and the process continues.

It was called the Variable Number of Tandem Repeats (VNTR). The technique, as used earlier, involved Southern blot hybridisation using radiolabeled VNTR as a probe. 131905.subject: Zoology
131905.text:
In a transcription unit, the DNA strand that has the promoter located at its 5' end has the following sequence:

5' CGATCGAT 3'

What will be the sequence of the mRNA transcribed from this transcription unit?
131905.sol:
In a transcription unit, the promoter is located towards the 5' end (upstream) of the structural gene, and this reference is made with respect to the polarity of the coding strand. Therefore, the DNA strand with the promoter at its 5' end is the coding strand.

The coding strand has the sequence 5' CGATCGAT 3'.

The mRNA transcribed from a transcription unit has the exact same sequence and polarity as the coding strand, with the only difference being the presence of Uracil (U) in RNA instead of Thymine (T) in DNA.

Replacing T with U in the coding strand gives the mRNA sequence: 5' CGAUCGAU 3'.

Options 1 and 2 are incorrect because they represent the sequence complementary to the coding strand (i.e., the mRNA sequence if the given strand were the template). Option 4 is incorrect because it has the wrong polarity.

Answer: 5' CGAUCGAU 3'

132184.subject: Zoology
132184.text: Where are the two alleles of a gene pair located?
options: On homologous sites on homologous chromosomes
132184.sol: In 1900, three Scientists (de Vries, Correns and von Tschermak) independently rediscovered Mendel’s results on the inheritance of characters. Also, by this time due to advancements in microscopy that were taking place, scientists were able to carefully observe cell division. This led to the discovery of structures in the nucleus that appeared to double and divide just before each cell division. These were called chromosomes (colored bodies, as they were visualized by staining). By 1902, the chromosome movement during meiosis had been worked out. Walter Sutton and Theodore Boveri noted that the behavior of chromosomes was parallel to the behavior of genes and used chromosome movement (Figure 4.8) to explain Mendel’s laws (Table 4.3). Recall that you have studied the behavior of chromosomes during mitosis (equational division) and during meiosis (reduction division). The important things to remember are that chromosomes as well as genes occur in pairs. The two alleles of a gene pair are located on homologous sites on homologous chromosomes

132463.subject: Zoology
132463.text:
In a genetic cross, the recombination frequencies between three linked genes $A$, $B$ and $C$ are as follows:
Between $A$ and $B$: $9\%$
Between $A$ and $C$: $17\%$
Between $B$ and $C$: $8\%$

Based on this data, what is the correct linear sequence of these genes on the chromosome?
132463.sol:
Alfred Sturtevant used the frequency of recombination between gene pairs on the same chromosome as a measure of the distance between genes. $1\%$ recombination frequency is equal to $1$ map unit.

Given recombination frequencies:
Distance between $A$ and $C$ = $17$ map units
Distance between $A$ and $B$ = $9$ map units
Distance between $B$ and $C$ = $8$ map units

The maximum distance is between genes $A$ and $C$ ($17$ map units), meaning they are located at the two ends of the sequence. The sum of the distances between $A-B$ and $B-C$ ($9 + 8 = 17$) equals the distance between $A-C$. Therefore, gene $B$ is located exactly between gene $A$ and gene $C$. The correct linear sequence is $A-B-C$.

Answer: $A-B-C$

132947.subject: Zoology
132947.text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Flippers of penguins and dolphins are considered homologous structures.
Reason (R): They have different anatomical origins but evolved to perform similar functions due to convergent evolution.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Assertion is false but Reason is true.
132947.sol:
The Assertion is false because the flippers of penguins (birds) and dolphins (mammals) are analogous structures, not homologous. They do not share a common ancestor with these specific flipper structures.

The Reason is true. Analogous structures arise when organisms with different anatomical origins adapt to similar habitats or lifestyles, evolving structures that perform similar functions (like swimming in this case). This evolutionary process is known as convergent evolution.

Therefore, Assertion is false but Reason is true.

Answer: Assertion is false but Reason is true.

135414.subject: Zoology
135414.text:
Match List I with List II.

List I (Organisms)List II (Population Interaction)
A. Ophrys and beeI. Mutualism
B. Fig and waspII. Commensalism
C. Cuckoo and crowIII. Brood parasitism
D. Cattle egret and grazing cattleIV. Sexual deceit

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
135414.sol:
The Mediterranean orchid Ophrys employs 'sexual deceit' to get pollinated by a species of bee. One petal of its flower bears an uncanny resemblance to the female bee.

Fig and wasp exhibit mutualism. The wasp pollinates the fig inflorescence while searching for suitable egg-laying sites, and the fig offers developing seeds as food for the wasp larvae.

Cuckoo and crow exhibit brood parasitism, where the parasitic bird (cuckoo) lays its eggs in the nest of its host (crow).

Cattle egret and grazing cattle show commensalism. The egrets benefit by catching insects flushed out by the cattle as they move, while the cattle are neither harmed nor benefited.

Thus, the correct match is A-IV, B-I, C-III, D-II.

Answer: A-IV, B-I, C-III, D-II

303165.subject: Physics
303165.chapter: Centre of Mass, Linear momentum, Collision
303165.text: A ball of mass $m$ is dropped onto a floor from a certain height. The collision is perfectly elastic, causing the ball to rebound to the same height and fall again. Determine the average force exerted by the ball on the floor over a long time interval.
303165.sol:
Let the ball be dropped from a height $h$.

The velocity of the ball just before hitting the floor is $v = \sqrt{2gh}$.

Since the collision is perfectly elastic, the ball rebounds with the same speed $v$.

The change in momentum of the ball during one collision is $\Delta p = mv - (-mv) = 2mv$.

The time interval between two successive collisions is the time taken by the ball to go up to height $h$ and fall back to the floor, which is $T = \dfrac{2v}{g}$.

The average force exerted by the floor on the ball is $F_{avg} = \dfrac{\Delta p}{T} = \dfrac{2mv}{\dfrac{2v}{g}} = mg$.

By Newton's third law, the average force exerted by the ball on the floor is equal in magnitude, which is $mg$.

303195.chapter: Centre of Mass, Linear momentum, Collision
303195.text: As depicted in the figure, two blocks of masses $m_1$ and $m_2$ are joined by a spring having spring constant $k$. The block of mass $m_2$ is subjected to a sharp impulse such that it gains a velocity $v_0$ towards the right. Find the velocity of the centre of mass.
303195.sol:
Initial velocity of block $m_1$, $v_1 = 0$.

Initial velocity of block $m_2$, $v_2 = v_0$.

The velocity of the centre of mass of the system is given by:

$v_{cm} = \dfrac{m_1 v_1 + m_2 v_2}{m_1 + m_2}$

Substituting the values:

$v_{cm} = \dfrac{m_1(0) + m_2(v_0)}{m_1 + m_2}$

$v_{cm} = \dfrac{m_2 v_0}{m_1 + m_2}$

Since there is no net external force acting on the system in the horizontal direction after the impulse, the velocity of the centre of mass remains constant.
